title: GitHub - aleph-void/LLM-Usage-Desktop-Widget: A Desktop Widget for Linux / Windows / MacOS that shows you your current LLM usage levels
excerpt: A Desktop Widget for Linux / Windows / MacOS that shows you your current LLM usage levels - aleph-void/LLM-Usage-Desktop-Widget
content_html:
Shows your Claude and Codex plan usage limits (session / weekly windows, model-scoped limits, and time until each resets) where your system status icons live:

Linux (Ubuntu) macOS Windows
OS Where it appears What it shows
Linux Top bar / panel, next to Wi-Fi and sound (AppIndicator) Icon + Claude 99% Codex 13%; click for details
macOS Menu bar, top right Gauge icon + Claude 99% Codex 13%; click for details
Windows An empty spot on the taskbar, plus a tray icon Claude 99% Codex 13% on the taskbar and a two-bar gauge icon; click either for details

The dropdown lists every limit with its percentage and reset countdown, plus Refresh now, links to each provider's usage page, and Quit. Bars and icons turn amber at 75% and red at 90% (or whatever severity the provider reports). If a refresh fails, the last numbers are kept and marked stale.

There is also a floating always-on-top window (--widget) for desktops without a tray.

It reuses the logins that Claude Code (claude) and the Codex CLI (codex) already store on your machine, so there is nothing to configure. Credentials are only read, never modified, and each token is sent only to the provider that issued it.

Provider Credentials read from Endpoint
Claude macOS Keychain Claude Code-credentials, else ~/.claude/.credentials.json ($CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR) api.anthropic.com/api/oauth/usage
Codex ~/.codex/auth.json ($CODEX_HOME) chatgpt.com/backend-api/wham/usage
Bedrock Your AWS credentials (profile, SSO, env vars), via boto3 AWS Budgets, Cost Explorer, CloudWatch
Vertex Google Application Default Credentials (gcloud auth application-default login) Cloud Monitoring, BigQuery billing export
Azure The Azure CLI login (az login), or azure-identity if installed Azure Monitor, Cost Management, Consumption budgets

These are the same internal endpoints the official CLIs use for their /usage and /status screens. They are undocumented and may change; if a provider shows an error after an update, check the parser for that provider in usage_widget.py.

Install

First log in to each CLI once with your subscription: claude → /login, and codex login. Each installer puts the app where it belongs for the OS, starts it right away, and starts it again every time you log in.

Option 1: packaged installers (no Python needed on macOS / Windows)

Download from the GitHub release (built by .github/workflows/build-installers.yml):

OS File Notes
Linux (Debian/Ubuntu) llm-usage-widget_<ver>_all.deb sudo apt install ./llm-usage-widget_*.deb. Starts right away for every logged-in user, and at login via /etc/xdg/autostart.
macOS LLM-Usage-Widget-<ver>-macos-arm64.dmg (Apple Silicon) or -x86_64.dmg (Intel) Open it and run Install LLM Usage Widget.pkg, which installs /Applications/LLM Usage.app plus a login LaunchAgent. Release builds are signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple.
Windows LLM-Usage-Widget-<ver>-windows-setup.exe Per-user install, no admin rights needed. "Start automatically when I sign in" is ticked by default. The build is unsigned, so SmartScreen may warn: click More info → Run anyway. Uninstall from Settings → Apps, the Uninstall LLM Usage Widget Start Menu entry, or by running the setup .exe with /uninstall (add /VERYSILENT to skip the prompts). Settings in %APPDATA%\llm-usage-widget are kept.

To uninstall on macOS, run Uninstall LLM Usage Widget.pkg from the same disk image (it asks for an administrator password), or run the copy of the uninstaller inside the app:

sudo "/Applications/LLM Usage.app/Contents/Resources/uninstall.sh"

Either one stops the widget for every logged-in user and removes the app, its LaunchAgent and the package receipt. Settings in ~/Library/Application Support/llm-usage-widget are left in place.

On Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt remove llm-usage-widget.

Option 2: install scripts (from a checkout of this repo)

OS Install Uninstall
Linux / macOS ./install.sh ./install.sh --uninstall
Windows double-click install.cmd (or powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File install.ps1) uninstall.cmd
  • Linux: copies to ~/.local/share/llm-usage-widget, adds an app-menu launcher and ~/.config/autostart/llm-usage-widget.desktop. Uses the system Python's PyGObject and AppIndicator (preinstalled on Ubuntu; the script prints the package command for your distro if they're missing). On GNOME the AppIndicator extension must be enabled (the default on Ubuntu; elsewhere install "AppIndicator and KStatusNotifierItem Support"). KDE, XFCE, Cinnamon and others work out of the box, though some panels show only the icon, not the text label.
  • macOS: needs Python 3.9+ (python.org or Homebrew). Copies to ~/Library/Application Support/llm-usage-widget with its own virtualenv and registers ~/Library/LaunchAgents/local.llm-usage-widget.plist. Logs go to ~/Library/Logs/llm-usage-widget.log.
  • Windows: needs Python 3.9+ from python.org. Copies to %LOCALAPPDATA%\llm-usage-widget with its own virtualenv and adds Start Menu and Startup shortcuts.

On macOS the first run may ask for Keychain access to Claude Code-credentials; choose Always Allow. On Windows the numbers are drawn on the taskbar itself: left of the ^ arrow when there is room, otherwise in the next empty gap (with centered taskbar buttons, usually left of Start), on two smaller lines if that is what fits. It never covers taskbar buttons; if the taskbar is completely full it hides until there is room. Windows has no API for text in the taskbar, so this is a small always-on-top window that follows the taskbar and steps aside for full-screen apps and an auto-hidden or vertical taskbar. Turn it off with Show usage on the taskbar in the menu. The tray icon may be tucked into the overflow (^) menu; drag it onto the taskbar to keep it visible.

To keep the numbers out of sight, choose Collapse to logo in the menu: the top bar, menu bar or taskbar then shows only the Aleph Void logo (on Windows the taskbar text is hidden and the tray icon becomes the logo). The numbers are still in the menu; choose it again to bring them back.

Running from source

/usr/bin/python3 usage_widget.py               # Linux (system Python, for PyGObject)
python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt     # macOS / Windows: pystray + Pillow
python3 usage_widget.py                         # Windows: pythonw usage_widget.py (no console window)

Only one copy runs at a time; starting a second one exits immediately.

Options

usage_widget.py                  # tray / top bar / menu bar (default)
usage_widget.py --widget         # floating always-on-top window instead
usage_widget.py --widget --framed    # ...with a normal title bar
usage_widget.py --once           # print usage in the terminal and exit
usage_widget.py --interval 300   # refresh every 5 minutes (default 180 s, min 60 s)

Cutoff quotas

Each provider can have its own cutoff: a percentage of its fullest limit at which the widget stops the CLIs that use that provider's quota. Choose one from Stop Claude at, Stop Codex at, etc. in the menu (Off, or every 5% from above the provider's current usage up to 95%, since a lower one would be reached at once). A cutoff chosen in the menu belongs to the account that is signed in: the Claude account and organization in ~/.claude.json, the ChatGPT account in ~/.codex/auth.json, the AWS account, the Google Cloud projects or the Azure subscription and resources. So with synced settings, a computer signed in to a different account is not affected. You can also set any value from 1 to 100 in config.json, where a plain number applies to any account:

"cutoff": {"Claude": {"<account uuid>/<organization uuid>": 95}, "Codex": 90}

On the first refresh that finds a provider at or over its cutoff, the widget stops every running process of that provider's CLI: claude for Claude, codex for Codex, and whichever of the two runs on it for Bedrock, Vertex AI and Azure (these need a budget, since that is their only limit with a percentage). The menu then shows ⛔ Cutoff 95% reached — stopped 2 claude processes; cutoff cleared. The cutoff turns itself off once it is reached, so you can start the CLI again; set a new cutoff if you want another one. The Claude and Codex desktop apps are never stopped. Usage is only checked on each refresh (every 3 minutes by default), so a busy session can go a little past the cutoff before it is stopped.

With synced settings, a cutoff set on one computer applies to every computer signed in to the same account, and each of them stops its own CLIs when it is reached (if it is running the widget and sees that within an hour).

Settings sync

On macOS and Windows the settings, including each provider's cutoff, sync between your computers through iCloud Drive and OneDrive, in an llm-usage-widget folder. When a computer has both, the settings go to both, so it also links a Mac that only has iCloud with a PC that only has OneDrive; the most recently saved copy wins. This needs nothing but iCloud Drive (or iCloud for Windows) or OneDrive being signed in; otherwise the settings stay on this computer, and the first time the widget finds a cloud folder it copies them there. The window position, Show usage on the taskbar and Collapse to logo are per computer and are not synced. macOS may ask once whether the widget may access iCloud Drive or OneDrive.

A full copy is also kept in the local config.json, which is used whenever no cloud folder is available. To edit settings by hand while syncing, edit a copy in a cloud folder. To stop syncing on one computer, add "sync": false to its local config.json. Uninstalling leaves the cloud copies in place.

Update notifications

Once a day the widget asks GitHub for the latest release (drafts and pre-releases don't count). When it is newer than the running copy, the menu starts with Update available: v1.2.3, which opens the release page, and the tooltip (the ⬆ v1.2.3 link in the floating widget's header) says so too. A desktop notification announces each new version once: Notification Center on macOS, a notification-area balloon on Windows, notify-send on Linux (from libnotify-bin, if installed). The floating widget on Windows has no notification, only the menu item and header link. The answer is cached in cloud-cache.json, so restarts don't ask again; if GitHub can't be reached, the widget tries again an hour later and otherwise carries on as usual. To turn the check off, add this to config.json:

"update_check": false

Expired logins

Claude Code and Codex refresh their own tokens while you use them. If you haven't used one for a while, its access token may expire and the widget will say so. Open that CLI once and the widget picks up the new token on its next refresh. The widget deliberately does not refresh tokens itself, because rotating the refresh token would log the CLI out.

Known issue: Ubuntu with GNOME 50

The Ubuntu AppIndicators extension shipped with GNOME 50 comes up half-broken at login: until it is reloaded, apps that start after its initial bus scan get No such method "RegisterStatusNotifierItem" and don't appear (this also hits Remmina, update-notifier, etc.). Apps already running during that scan do appear, so starting the widget at login usually works. install.sh detects the broken state and reloads the extension once so the icon appears immediately. If the icon is missing, reload it by hand:

gnome-extensions disable ubuntu-appindicators@ubuntu.com && gnome-extensions enable ubuntu-appindicators@ubuntu.com

Building the installers

The GitHub Actions workflow builds every installer on its own OS. Push a tag matching __version__ in usage_widget.py (e.g. v1.0.0) to build them and attach them to a release, or run the workflow by hand to download them as build artifacts. To build locally on each OS:

packaging/linux/build-deb.sh                                   # Linux → dist/*.deb
python3 -m pip install pyinstaller -r requirements.txt
packaging/macos/build-pkg.sh                                   # macOS → dist/*.dmg
powershell -File packaging\windows\build.ps1                   # Windows → dist\*-setup.exe (needs Inno Setup 6)

To sign the macOS build locally, set CODESIGN_IDENTITY (a "Developer ID Application" identity) and INSTALLER_SIGN_IDENTITY ("Developer ID Installer"). The app is signed with the hardened runtime and a secure timestamp, which is what notarization requires, and the disk image is signed with the same identity. Then notarize and staple the disk image, which covers the pkgs inside it:

xcrun notarytool submit dist/*.dmg --keychain-profile <profile> --wait
xcrun stapler staple dist/*.dmg

In CI, the macOS job signs, notarizes and staples the disk image when these repository secrets are set. A tag release fails without them:

Secret Contents
MAC_CERT_P12_BASE64 / MAC_CERT_PASSWORD The Developer ID Application certificate and private key, as a base64-encoded .p12, and its export password
MAC_INSTALLER_CERT_P12_BASE64 / MAC_INSTALLER_CERT_PASSWORD The same for the Developer ID Installer certificate
AC_API_KEY_P8_BASE64 / AC_API_KEY_ID / AC_API_ISSUER_ID An App Store Connect API key (the base64-encoded .p8), its key ID and issuer ID, used by notarytool

Code signing (Windows)

The workflow Authenticode-signs LLMUsageWidget.exe and the setup .exe with Azure Trusted Signing (the same setup as Virux), timestamps both, and checks the signatures before uploading. A tag build fails rather than publish an unsigned installer; a manual run without the secrets builds unsigned with a warning. It needs these repository (or organization) secrets:

Secret What it is
AZURE_TENANT_ID Entra ID tenant of the app registration that signs
AZURE_CLIENT_ID That app registration's client ID
AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET A client secret for it; also how the workflow decides whether to sign
AZ_TS_ENDPOINT The Trusted Signing account's regional endpoint, e.g. https://eus.codesigning.azure.net
AZ_TS_ACCOUNT Trusted Signing account name
AZ_TS_PROFILE Certificate profile name

The app registration needs the Trusted Signing Certificate Profile Signer role on the account.

Publisher name only, no address. Windows shows the certificate's common name, the validated organization name ("Aleph Void LLC"), as the publisher in SmartScreen, the UAC prompt and the file's Digital Signatures tab. Create the Public Trust certificate profile with Include street address and Include postal code both unticked (the default) so the certificate carries no address. City, state and country are always part of a Public Trust certificate's details and can't be removed. packaging/windows/verify-signature.ps1 fails the build if a signature is invalid, not timestamped, or its certificate includes a street address or postal code. Run it on a downloaded installer to check it yourself:

powershell -File packaging\windows\verify-signature.ps1 .\LLM-Usage-Widget-<ver>-windows-setup.exe

/uninstall runs from the same signed setup .exe. The uninstaller that Inno Setup writes into the install folder at install time is not signed. It runs without elevation (the install is per-user), so Windows doesn't show a publisher prompt for it.

Amazon Bedrock (and bedrock-mantle)

If Claude Code or Codex runs on Amazon Bedrock instead of a subscription, there are no session or weekly limits to show. Instead the widget adds a Bedrock section that shows:

  • Budget: spend against an AWS Budget as a percentage bar that resets with the budget period. This only appears if you name a budget (see below).
  • This month: month-to-date spend for every service with "Bedrock" in its name, from Cost Explorer. Third-party models such as Claude are billed as Marketplace services named like Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Amazon Bedrock Edition), and these are included.
  • Tokens today: input and output tokens since local midnight, from CloudWatch. This covers both the bedrock-runtime endpoint (AWS/Bedrock) and the OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible bedrock-mantle endpoint (AWS/BedrockMantle).

The section turns on automatically when Claude Code's settings set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK (or an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL containing bedrock), or when a base_url in ~/.codex/config.toml points at Bedrock. The AWS profile and region come from the same place: AWS_PROFILE and AWS_REGION in Claude Code's env block, or the region in Codex's base_url. In that case the Claude or Codex section is hidden if that CLI has no subscription login. To override any of this, add a bedrock entry to config.json in the widget's config folder (~/.config/llm-usage-widget/ on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/llm-usage-widget/ on macOS, %APPDATA%\llm-usage-widget\ on Windows; a cloud folder when settings sync):

{
  "bedrock": {
    "profile": "work",
    "regions": ["us-east-1", "us-west-2"],
    "budget": "bedrock-monthly",
    "cost_explorer": true,
    "cost_interval": 21600,
    "metrics_interval": 900
  }
}

Use "bedrock": true to turn the section on with the defaults, or false to hide it.

This needs boto3: it is in requirements.txt and in the macOS and Windows packages. On Linux, run sudo apt install python3-boto3 (or install it for the system Python another way). The IAM identity needs ce:GetCostAndUsage, cloudwatch:GetMetricData, and, for a budget, budgets:ViewBudget and sts:GetCallerIdentity. If a permission is missing, only that row shows an error. If the credentials have expired (for example an SSO session), the section says to run aws sso login.

Cost: Cost Explorer charges $0.01 per request and its data only updates a few times a day, so spend (and the budget) is fetched at most every cost_interval seconds (6 h by default, about $1.20 a month). Token counts are fetched every metrics_interval seconds (15 min). Both are cached in cloud-cache.json next to config.json, so restarts don't refetch them, and Refresh now doesn't bypass the cache either. Billing data can lag by a day or more, so don't treat this as a spending alarm.

Google Vertex AI

If Claude Code or Codex runs on Vertex AI, the widget adds a Vertex section instead:

  • Tokens today: input and output tokens since local midnight from Cloud Monitoring (aiplatform.googleapis.com/publisher/online_serving/token_count). This counts every publisher model in the project (Claude, Gemini and others), not only the ones the CLIs use.
  • This month: month-to-date spend, after credits, for Vertex AI and partner models such as Claude. Google has no API that reports current spend, so this needs a Cloud Billing export to BigQuery and its table name in billing_table. If you also set budget (an amount per month, in the billing currency), the row becomes a percentage bar.

The section turns on when Claude Code's settings set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX, or a base_url in ~/.codex/config.toml points at aiplatform.googleapis.com. The project comes from ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID or the projects/<id>/ part of that URL. Overrides go in config.json:

{
  "vertex": {
    "projects": ["my-project"],
    "billing_table": "my-project.billing.gcp_billing_export_v1_XXXXXX_XXXXXX_XXXXXX",
    "budget": 500,
    "cost_interval": 21600,
    "metrics_interval": 900
  }
}

Use "vertex": true or false to force the section on or off. Credentials are the Application Default Credentials from gcloud auth application-default login (or $GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS), refreshed directly with Google. For service-account or other ADC types the widget uses the google-auth package if it is installed, else gcloud auth print-access-token. The identity needs monitoring.timeSeries.list (Monitoring Viewer) and, for spend, BigQuery Job User plus read access to the export dataset. The billing query is run in the first project and scans the current month of the export table, which usually costs nothing or close to it.

Azure OpenAI and Microsoft Foundry

If Codex (or Claude Code, through Microsoft Foundry) runs on Azure, the widget adds an Azure section:

  • Budget: spend against an Azure budget as a percentage bar. This only appears if you name a budget.
  • This month: month-to-date actual cost of the Azure OpenAI / Foundry resources, from Cost Management.
  • Tokens today: prompt and completion tokens since local midnight, from Azure Monitor.

The section turns on when a base_url in ~/.codex/config.toml points at <resource>.openai.azure.com, <resource>.cognitiveservices.azure.com or <resource>.services.ai.azure.com, or Claude Code's settings set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY (the resource comes from ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_RESOURCE or ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_BASE_URL). The widget finds those resources in your subscription. Overrides go in config.json:

{
  "azure": {
    "subscription": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000",
    "resources": ["my-openai", "/subscriptions/.../providers/Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/other"],
    "budget": "ai-monthly",
    "cost_management": true,
    "cost_interval": 21600,
    "metrics_interval": 900
  }
}

resources takes resource names or full resource IDs. With "azure": true and no resources, every Azure OpenAI and AI Services resource in the subscription is included. budget is a budget name at subscription scope, or a budget's full resource ID for one on a resource group. Without subscription, the Azure CLI's current one is used (or all of them, with azure-identity). Credentials come from az login, or from the azure-identity package's DefaultAzureCredential if the CLI isn't available. The identity needs Reader on the resources (with Monitoring Reader) and Cost Management Reader on the subscription. Cost data is cached like Bedrock's: Cost Management is free but throttled, and only updates a few times a day.

Adding a provider

Write a fetch_<name>() that returns a ProviderUsage and add it to PROVIDERS, then add tests for it under tests/ (see tests/test_codex.py for the pattern: canned responses, no network).

Running the tests

python3 -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python3 -m pytest                  # Linux without a display: xvfb-run -a python3 -m pytest
python3 -m pytest --cov            # with a coverage report

The tests never touch the network or your real logins: each one runs against an empty temporary home directory, and the provider APIs, AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, GTK/AppIndicator, pystray and Win32 are faked. The Tk tests are skipped when there is no display. GitHub Actions runs the suite on every pull request and push to main (.github/workflows/tests.yml) on Linux, macOS and Windows with Python 3.9 to 3.14, plus Ruff and ShellCheck, and installs the .deb on Ubuntu to run the tests on the system Python.

Usage is only checked on each refresh (every 3 minutes by default), so a busy session can go a little past the cutoff before it is stopped. With synced settings, a cutoff set on one computer applies to every computer signed in to the same account, and each of them stops its own CLIs when it is reached (if it is running the widget and sees that within an hour). Settings sync On macOS and Windows the settings, including each provider's cutoff, sync between your computers through iCloud Drive and OneDrive, in an llm-usage-widget folder. When a computer has both, the settings go to both, so it also links a Mac that only has iCloud with a PC that only has OneDrive; the most recently saved copy wins. This needs nothing but iCloud Drive (or iCloud for Windows) or OneDrive being signed in; otherwise the settings stay on this computer, and the first time the widget finds a cloud folder it copies them there. The window position, Show usage on the taskbar and Collapse to logo are per computer and are not synced. macOS may ask once whether the widget may access iCloud Drive or OneDrive. A full copy is also kept in the local config.json, which is used whenever no cloud folder is available. To edit settings by hand while syncing, edit a copy in a cloud folder. To stop syncing on one computer, add "sync": false to its local config.json. Uninstalling leaves the cloud copies in place. Update notifications Once a day the widget asks GitHub for the latest release (drafts and pre-releases don't count). When it is newer than the running copy, the menu starts with Update available: v1.2.3, which opens the release page, and the tooltip (the ⬆ v1.2.3 link in the floating widget's header) says so too. A desktop notification announces each new version once: Notification Center on macOS, a notification-area balloon on Windows, notify-send on Linux (from libnotify-bin, if installed). The floating widget on Windows has no notification, only the menu item and header link. The answer is cached in cloud-cache.json, so restarts don't ask again; if GitHub can't be reached, the widget tries again an hour later and otherwise carries on as usual. To turn the check off, add this to config.json: "update_check": false Expired logins Claude Code and Codex refresh their own tokens while you use them. If you haven't used one for a while, its access token may expire and the widget will say so. Open that CLI once and the widget picks up the new token on its next refresh. The widget deliberately does not refresh tokens itself, because rotating the refresh token would log the CLI out. Known issue: Ubuntu with GNOME 50 The Ubuntu AppIndicators extension shipped with GNOME 50 comes up half-broken at login: until it is reloaded, apps that start after its initial bus scan get No such method "RegisterStatusNotifierItem" and don't appear (this also hits Remmina, update-notifier, etc.). Apps already running during that scan do appear, so starting the widget at login usually works. install.sh detects the broken state and reloads the extension once so the icon appears immediately. If the icon is missing, reload it by hand: gnome-extensions disable ubuntu-appindicators@ubuntu.com && gnome-extensions enable ubuntu-appindicators@ubuntu.com Building the installers The GitHub Actions workflow builds every installer on its own OS. Push a tag matching __version__ in usage_widget.py (e.g. v1.0.0) to build them and attach them to a release, or run the workflow by hand to download them as build artifacts. To build locally on each OS: packaging/linux/build-deb.sh # Linux → dist/*.deb python3 -m pip install pyinstaller -r requirements.txt packaging/macos/build-pkg.sh # macOS → dist/*.dmg powershell -File packaging\windows\build.ps1 # Windows → dist\*-setup.exe (needs Inno Setup 6) To sign the macOS build locally, set CODESIGN_IDENTITY (a "Developer ID Application" identity) and INSTALLER_SIGN_IDENTITY ("Developer ID Installer"). The app is signed with the hardened runtime and a secure timestamp, which is what notarization requires, and the disk image is signed with the same identity. Then notarize and staple the disk image, which covers the pkgs inside it: xcrun notarytool submit dist/*.dmg --keychain-profile <profile> --wait xcrun stapler staple dist/*.dmg In CI, the macOS job signs, notarizes and staples the disk image when these repository secrets are set. A tag release fails without them: Secret Contents MAC_CERT_P12_BASE64 / MAC_CERT_PASSWORD The Developer ID Application certificate and private key, as a base64-encoded .p12, and its export password MAC_INSTALLER_CERT_P12_BASE64 / MAC_INSTALLER_CERT_PASSWORD The same for the Developer ID Installer certificate AC_API_KEY_P8_BASE64 / AC_API_KEY_ID / AC_API_ISSUER_ID An App Store Connect API key (the base64-encoded .p8), its key ID and issuer ID, used by notarytool Code signing (Windows) The workflow Authenticode-signs LLMUsageWidget.exe and the setup .exe with Azure Trusted Signing (the same setup as Virux), timestamps both, and checks the signatures before uploading. A tag build fails rather than publish an unsigned installer; a manual run without the secrets builds unsigned with a warning. It needs these repository (or organization) secrets: Secret What it is AZURE_TENANT_ID Entra ID tenant of the app registration that signs AZURE_CLIENT_ID That app registration's client ID AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET A client secret for it; also how the workflow decides whether to sign AZ_TS_ENDPOINT The Trusted Signing account's regional endpoint, e.g. https://eus.codesigning.azure.net AZ_TS_ACCOUNT Trusted Signing account name AZ_TS_PROFILE Certificate profile name The app registration needs the Trusted Signing Certificate Profile Signer role on the account. Publisher name only, no address. Windows shows the certificate's common name, the validated organization name ("Aleph Void LLC"), as the publisher in SmartScreen, the UAC prompt and the file's Digital Signatures tab. Create the Public Trust certificate profile with Include street address and Include postal code both unticked (the default) so the certificate carries no address. City, state and country are always part of a Public Trust certificate's details and can't be removed. packaging/windows/verify-signature.ps1 fails the build if a signature is invalid, not timestamped, or its certificate includes a street address or postal code. Run it on a downloaded installer to check it yourself: powershell -File packaging\windows\verify-signature.ps1 .\LLM-Usage-Widget-<ver>-windows-setup.exe /uninstall runs from the same signed setup .exe. The uninstaller that Inno Setup writes into the install folder at install time is not signed. It runs without elevation (the install is per-user), so Windows doesn't show a publisher prompt for it. Amazon Bedrock (and bedrock-mantle) If Claude Code or Codex runs on Amazon Bedrock instead of a subscription, there are no session or weekly limits to show. Instead the widget adds a Bedrock section that shows: Budget: spend against an AWS Budget as a percentage bar that resets with the budget period. This only appears if you name a budget (see below). This month: month-to-date spend for every service with "Bedrock" in its name, from Cost Explorer. Third-party models such as Claude are billed as Marketplace services named like Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Amazon Bedrock Edition), and these are included. Tokens today: input and output tokens since local midnight, from CloudWatch. This covers both the bedrock-runtime endpoint (AWS/Bedrock) and the OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible bedrock-mantle endpoint (AWS/BedrockMantle). The section turns on automatically when Claude Code's settings set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK (or an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL containing bedrock), or when a base_url in ~/.codex/config.toml points at Bedrock. The AWS profile and region come from the same place: AWS_PROFILE and AWS_REGION in Claude Code's env block, or the region in Codex's base_url. In that case the Claude or Codex section is hidden if that CLI has no subscription login. To override any of this, add a bedrock entry to config.json in the widget's config folder (~/.config/llm-usage-widget/ on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/llm-usage-widget/ on macOS, %APPDATA%\llm-usage-widget\ on Windows; a cloud folder when settings sync): { "bedrock": { "profile": "work", "regions": ["us-east-1", "us-west-2"], "budget": "bedrock-monthly", "cost_explorer": true, "cost_interval": 21600, "metrics_interval": 900 } } Use "bedrock": true to turn the section on with the defaults, or false to hide it. This needs boto3: it is in requirements.txt and in the macOS and Windows packages. On Linux, run sudo apt install python3-boto3 (or install it for the system Python another way). The IAM identity needs ce:GetCostAndUsage, cloudwatch:GetMetricData, and, for a budget, budgets:ViewBudget and sts:GetCallerIdentity. If a permission is missing, only that row shows an error. If the credentials have expired (for example an SSO session), the section says to run aws sso login. Cost: Cost Explorer charges $0.01 per request and its data only updates a few times a day, so spend (and the budget) is fetched at most every cost_interval seconds (6 h by default, about $1.20 a month). Token counts are fetched every metrics_interval seconds (15 min). Both are cached in cloud-cache.json next to config.json, so restarts don't refetch them, and Refresh now doesn't bypass the cache either. Billing data can lag by a day or more, so don't treat this as a spending alarm. Google Vertex AI If Claude Code or Codex runs on Vertex AI, the widget adds a Vertex section instead: Tokens today: input and output tokens since local midnight from Cloud Monitoring (aiplatform.googleapis.com/publisher/online_serving/token_count). This counts every publisher model in the project (Claude, Gemini and others), not only the ones the CLIs use. This month: month-to-date spend, after credits, for Vertex AI and partner models such as Claude. Google has no API that reports current spend, so this needs a Cloud Billing export to BigQuery and its table name in billing_table. If you also set budget (an amount per month, in the billing currency), the row becomes a percentage bar. The section turns on when Claude Code's settings set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX, or a base_url in ~/.codex/config.toml points at aiplatform.googleapis.com. The project comes from ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID or the projects/<id>/ part of that URL. Overrides go in config.json: { "vertex": { "projects": ["my-project"], "billing_table": "my-project.billing.gcp_billing_export_v1_XXXXXX_XXXXXX_XXXXXX", "budget": 500, "cost_interval": 21600, "metrics_interval": 900 } } Use "vertex": true or false to force the section on or off. Credentials are the Application Default Credentials from gcloud auth application-default login (or $GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS), refreshed directly with Google. For service-account or other ADC types the widget uses the google-auth package if it is installed, else gcloud auth print-access-token. The identity needs monitoring.timeSeries.list (Monitoring Viewer) and, for spend, BigQuery Job User plus read access to the export dataset. The billing query is run in the first project and scans the current month of the export table, which usually costs nothing or close to it. Azure OpenAI and Microsoft Foundry If Codex (or Claude Code, through Microsoft Foundry) runs on Azure, the widget adds an Azure section: Budget: spend against an Azure budget as a percentage bar. This only appears if you name a budget. This month: month-to-date actual cost of the Azure OpenAI / Foundry resources, from Cost Management. Tokens today: prompt and completion tokens since local midnight, from Azure Monitor. The section turns on when a base_url in ~/.codex/config.toml points at <resource>.openai.azure.com, <resource>.cognitiveservices.azure.com or <resource>.services.ai.azure.com, or Claude Code's settings set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY (the resource comes from ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_RESOURCE or ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_BASE_URL). The widget finds those resources in your subscription. Overrides go in config.json: { "azure": { "subscription": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "resources": ["my-openai", "/subscriptions/.../providers/Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/other"], "budget": "ai-monthly", "cost_management": true, "cost_interval": 21600, "metrics_interval": 900 } } resources takes resource names or full resource IDs. With "azure": true and no resources, every Azure OpenAI and AI Services resource in the subscription is included. budget is a budget name at subscription scope, or a budget's full resource ID for one on a resource group. Without subscription, the Azure CLI's current one is used (or all of them, with azure-identity). Credentials come from az login, or from the azure-identity package's DefaultAzureCredential if the CLI isn't available. The identity needs Reader on the resources (with Monitoring Reader) and Cost Management Reader on the subscription. Cost data is cached like Bedrock's: Cost Management is free but throttled, and only updates a few times a day. Adding a provider Write a fetch_<name>() that returns a ProviderUsage and add it to PROVIDERS, then add tests for it under tests/ (see tests/test_codex.py for the pattern: canned responses, no network). Running the tests python3 -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt python3 -m pytest # Linux without a display: xvfb-run -a python3 -m pytest python3 -m pytest --cov # with a coverage report The tests never touch the network or your real logins: each one runs against an empty temporary home directory, and the provider APIs, AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, GTK/AppIndicator, pystray and Win32 are faked. The Tk tests are skipped when there is no display. GitHub Actions runs the suite on every pull request and push to main (.github/workflows/tests.yml) on Linux, macOS and Windows with Python 3.9 to 3.14, plus Ruff and ShellCheck, and installs the .deb on Ubuntu to run the tests on the system Python. 安装

First log in to each CLI once with your subscription: claude → /login, and codex login. Each installer puts the app where it belongs for the OS, starts it right away, and starts it again every time you log in.

To keep the numbers out of sight, choose Collapse to logo in the menu: the top bar, menu bar or taskbar then shows only the Aleph Void logo (on Windows the taskbar text is hidden and the tray icon becomes the logo). The numbers are still in the menu; choose it again to bring them back.

Cutoff quotas

Each provider can have its own cutoff: a percentage of its fullest limit at which the widget stops the CLIs that use that provider's quota. Choose one from Stop Claude at, Stop Codex at, etc. in the menu (Off, or every 5% from above the provider's current usage up to 95%, since a lower one would be reached at once). A cutoff chosen in the menu belongs to the account that is signed in: the Claude account and organization in ~/.claude.json, the ChatGPT account in ~/.codex/auth.json, the AWS account, the Google Cloud projects or the Azure subscription and resources. So with synced settings, a computer signed in to a different account is not affected. You can also set any value from 1 to 100 in config.json, where a plain number applies to any account:

"cutoff": {"Claude": {"<account uuid>/<organization uuid>": 95}, "Codex": 90}

On the first refresh that finds a provider at or over its cutoff, the widget stops every running process of that provider's CLI: claude for Claude, codex for Codex, and whichever of the two runs on it for Bedrock, Vertex AI and Azure (these need a budget, since that is their only limit with a percentage). The menu then shows ⛔ Cutoff 95% reached — stopped 2 claude processes; cutoff cleared. The cutoff turns itself off once it is reached, so you can start the CLI again; set a new cutoff if you want another one. The Claude and Codex desktop apps are never stopped. Usage is only checked on each refresh (every 3 minutes by default), so a busy session can go a little past the cutoff before it is stopped.

With synced settings, a cutoff set on one computer applies to every computer signed in to the same account, and each of them stops its own CLIs when it is reached (if it is running the widget and sees that within an hour).

Settings sync

On macOS and Windows the settings, including each provider's cutoff, sync between your computers through iCloud Drive and OneDrive, in an llm-usage-widget folder. When a computer has both, the settings go to both, so it also links a Mac that only has iCloud with a PC that only has OneDrive; the most recently saved copy wins. This needs nothing but iCloud Drive (or iCloud for Windows) or OneDrive being signed in; otherwise the settings stay on this computer, and the first time the widget finds a cloud folder it copies them there. The window position, Show usage on the taskbar and Collapse to logo are per computer and are not synced. macOS may ask once whether the widget may access iCloud Drive or OneDrive.

A full copy is also kept in the local config.json, which is used whenever no cloud folder is available. To edit settings by hand while syncing, edit a copy in a cloud folder. To stop syncing on one computer, add "sync": false to its local config.json. Uninstalling leaves the cloud copies in place.

Update notifications

Once a day the widget asks GitHub for the latest release (drafts and pre-releases don't count). When it is newer than the running copy, the menu starts with Update available: v1.2.3, which opens the release page, and the tooltip (the ⬆ v1.2.3 link in the floating widget's header) says so too. A desktop notification announces each new version once: Notification Center on macOS, a notification-area balloon on Windows, notify-send on Linux (from libnotify-bin, if installed). The floating widget on Windows has no notification, only the menu item and header link. The answer is cached in cloud-cache.json, so restarts don't ask again; if GitHub can't be reached, the widget tries again an hour later and otherwise carries on as usual. To turn the check off, add this to config.json:

"update_check": false

Expired logins

Claude Code and Codex refresh their own tokens while you use them. If you haven't used one for a while, its access token may expire and the widget will say so. Open that CLI once and the widget picks up the new token on its next refresh. The widget deliberately does not refresh tokens itself, because rotating the refresh token would log the CLI out.

Known issue: Ubuntu with GNOME 50

The Ubuntu AppIndicators extension shipped with GNOME 50 comes up half-broken at login: until it is reloaded, apps that start after its initial bus scan get No such method "RegisterStatusNotifierItem" and don't appear (this also hits Remmina, update-notifier, etc.). Apps already running during that scan do appear, so starting the widget at login usually works. install.sh detects the broken state and reloads the extension once so the icon appears immediately. If the icon is missing, reload it by hand:

gnome-extensions disable ubuntu-appindicators@ubuntu.com && gnome-extensions enable ubuntu-appindicators@ubuntu.com

Building the installers

The GitHub Actions workflow builds every installer on its own OS. Push a tag matching __version__ in usage_widget.py (e.g. v1.0.0) to build them and attach them to a release, or run the workflow by hand to download them as build artifacts. To build locally on each OS:

packaging/linux/build-deb.sh                                   # Linux → dist/*.deb
python3 -m pip install pyinstaller -r requirements.txt
packaging/macos/build-pkg.sh                                   # macOS → dist/*.dmg
powershell -File packaging\windows\build.ps1                   # Windows → dist\*-setup.exe (needs Inno Setup 6)

To sign the macOS build locally, set CODESIGN_IDENTITY (a "Developer ID Application" identity) and INSTALLER_SIGN_IDENTITY ("Developer ID Installer"). The app is signed with the hardened runtime and a secure timestamp, which is what notarization requires, and the disk image is signed with the same identity. Then notarize and staple the disk image, which covers the pkgs inside it:

xcrun notarytool submit dist/*.dmg --keychain-profile <profile> --wait
xcrun stapler staple dist/*.dmg

In CI, the macOS job signs, notarizes and staples the disk image when these repository secrets are set. A tag release fails without them:

MAC_CERT_P12_BASE64 / MAC_CERT_PASSWORD The Developer ID Application certificate and private key, as a base64-encoded .p12, and its export password
MAC_INSTALLER_CERT_P12_BASE64 / MAC_INSTALLER_CERT_PASSWORD The same for the Developer ID Installer certificate
AC_API_KEY_P8_BASE64 / AC_API_KEY_ID / AC_API_ISSUER_ID An App Store Connect API key (the base64-encoded .p8), its key ID and issuer ID, used by notarytool

Code signing (Windows)

The workflow Authenticode-signs LLMUsageWidget.exe and the setup .exe with Azure Trusted Signing (the same setup as Virux), timestamps both, and checks the signatures before uploading. A tag build fails rather than publish an unsigned installer; a manual run without the secrets builds unsigned with a warning. It needs these repository (or organization) secrets:

The app registration needs the Trusted Signing Certificate Profile Signer role on the account.

Publisher name only, no address. Windows shows the certificate's common name, the validated organization name ("Aleph Void LLC"), as the publisher in SmartScreen, the UAC prompt and the file's Digital Signatures tab. Create the Public Trust certificate profile with Include street address and Include postal code both unticked (the default) so the certificate carries no address. City, state and country are always part of a Public Trust certificate's details and can't be removed. packaging/windows/verify-signature.ps1 fails the build if a signature is invalid, not timestamped, or its certificate includes a street address or postal code. Run it on a downloaded installer to check it yourself:

powershell -File packaging\windows\verify-signature.ps1 .\LLM-Usage-Widget-<ver>-windows-setup.exe

/uninstall runs from the same signed setup .exe. The uninstaller that Inno Setup writes into the install folder at install time is not signed. It runs without elevation (the install is per-user), so Windows doesn't show a publisher prompt for it.

Amazon Bedrock (and bedrock-mantle)

If Claude Code or Codex runs on Amazon Bedrock instead of a subscription, there are no session or weekly limits to show. Instead the widget adds a Bedrock section that shows:

  • Budget: spend against an AWS Budget as a percentage bar that resets with the budget period. This only appears if you name a budget (see below).
  • This month: month-to-date spend for every service with "Bedrock" in its name, from Cost Explorer. Third-party models such as Claude are billed as Marketplace services named like Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Amazon Bedrock Edition), and these are included.
  • Tokens today: input and output tokens since local midnight, from CloudWatch. This covers both the bedrock-runtime endpoint (AWS/Bedrock) and the OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible bedrock-mantle endpoint (AWS/BedrockMantle).

The section turns on automatically when Claude Code's settings set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK (or an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL containing bedrock), or when a base_url in ~/.codex/config.toml points at Bedrock. The AWS profile and region come from the same place: AWS_PROFILE and AWS_REGION in Claude Code's env block, or the region in Codex's base_url. In that case the Claude or Codex section is hidden if that CLI has no subscription login. To override any of this, add a bedrock entry to config.json in the widget's config folder (~/.config/llm-usage-widget/ on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/llm-usage-widget/ on macOS, %APPDATA%\llm-usage-widget\ on Windows; a cloud folder when settings sync):

{
  "bedrock": {
    "profile": "work",
    "regions": ["us-east-1", "us-west-2"],
    "budget": "bedrock-monthly",
    "cost_explorer": true,
    "cost_interval": 21600,
    "metrics_interval": 900
  }
}

Use "bedrock": true to turn the section on with the defaults, or false to hide it.

This needs boto3: it is in requirements.txt and in the macOS and Windows packages. On Linux, run sudo apt install python3-boto3 (or install it for the system Python another way). The IAM identity needs ce:GetCostAndUsage, cloudwatch:GetMetricData, and, for a budget, budgets:ViewBudget and sts:GetCallerIdentity. If a permission is missing, only that row shows an error. If the credentials have expired (for example an SSO session), the section says to run aws sso login.

Cost: Cost Explorer charges $0.01 per request and its data only updates a few times a day, so spend (and the budget) is fetched at most every cost_interval seconds (6 h by default, about $1.20 a month). Token counts are fetched every metrics_interval seconds (15 min). Both are cached in cloud-cache.json next to config.json, so restarts don't refetch them, and Refresh now doesn't bypass the cache either. Billing data can lag by a day or more, so don't treat this as a spending alarm.

If Claude Code or Codex runs on Vertex AI, the widget adds a Vertex section instead:

  • Tokens today: input and output tokens since local midnight from Cloud Monitoring (aiplatform.googleapis.com/publisher/online_serving/token_count). This counts every publisher model in the project (Claude, Gemini and others), not only the ones the CLIs use.
  • This month: month-to-date spend, after credits, for Vertex AI and partner models such as Claude. Google has no API that reports current spend, so this needs a Cloud Billing export to BigQuery and its table name in billing_table. If you also set budget (an amount per month, in the billing currency), the row becomes a percentage bar.

The section turns on when Claude Code's settings set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX, or a base_url in ~/.codex/config.toml points at aiplatform.googleapis.com. The project comes from ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID or the projects/<id>/ part of that URL. Overrides go in config.json:

{
  "vertex": {
    "projects": ["my-project"],
    "billing_table": "my-project.billing.gcp_billing_export_v1_XXXXXX_XXXXXX_XXXXXX",
    "budget": 500,
    "cost_interval": 21600,
    "metrics_interval": 900
  }
}

Use "vertex": true or false to force the section on or off. Credentials are the Application Default Credentials from gcloud auth application-default login (or $GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS), refreshed directly with Google. For service-account or other ADC types the widget uses the google-auth package if it is installed, else gcloud auth print-access-token. The identity needs monitoring.timeSeries.list (Monitoring Viewer) and, for spend, BigQuery Job User plus read access to the export dataset. The billing query is run in the first project and scans the current month of the export table, which usually costs nothing or close to it.

Azure OpenAI and Microsoft Foundry

If Codex (or Claude Code, through Microsoft Foundry) runs on Azure, the widget adds an Azure section:

  • Budget: spend against an Azure budget as a percentage bar. This only appears if you name a budget.
  • This month: month-to-date actual cost of the Azure OpenAI / Foundry resources, from Cost Management.
  • Tokens today: prompt and completion tokens since local midnight, from Azure Monitor.

The section turns on when a base_url in ~/.codex/config.toml points at <resource>.openai.azure.com, <resource>.cognitiveservices.azure.com or <resource>.services.ai.azure.com, or Claude Code's settings set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY (the resource comes from ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_RESOURCE or ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_BASE_URL). The widget finds those resources in your subscription. Overrides go in config.json:

{
  "azure": {
    "subscription": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000",
    "resources": ["my-openai", "/subscriptions/.../providers/Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/other"],
    "budget": "ai-monthly",
    "cost_management": true,
    "cost_interval": 21600,
    "metrics_interval": 900
  }
}

resources takes resource names or full resource IDs. With "azure": true and no resources, every Azure OpenAI and AI Services resource in the subscription is included. budget is a budget name at subscription scope, or a budget's full resource ID for one on a resource group. Without subscription, the Azure CLI's current one is used (or all of them, with azure-identity). Credentials come from az login, or from the azure-identity package's DefaultAzureCredential if the CLI isn't available. The identity needs Reader on the resources (with Monitoring Reader) and Cost Management Reader on the subscription. Cost data is cached like Bedrock's: Cost Management is free but throttled, and only updates a few times a day.

Adding a provider

Write a fetch_<name>() that returns a ProviderUsage and add it to PROVIDERS, then add tests for it under tests/ (see tests/test_codex.py for the pattern: canned responses, no network).

Running the tests

python3 -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python3 -m pytest                  # Linux without a display: xvfb-run -a python3 -m pytest
python3 -m pytest --cov            # with a coverage report

The tests never touch the network or your real logins: each one runs against an empty temporary home directory, and the provider APIs, AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, GTK/AppIndicator, pystray and Win32 are faked. The Tk tests are skipped when there is no display. GitHub Actions runs the suite on every pull request and push to main (.github/workflows/tests.yml) on Linux, macOS and Windows with Python 3.9 to 3.14, plus Ruff and ShellCheck, and installs the .deb on Ubuntu to run the tests on the system Python.
